title: Succession planning for senior staff roles — preparing for the unexpected
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals on succession planning for deputy principals, HODs, and other senior roles — reducing disruption when key staff leave.
body:
A deputy principal transferred with two weeks' notice. A long-serving head of department who suddenly resigns. A senior teacher who goes on extended medical leave. These events happen in every school eventually, and schools without any succession planning experience them as genuine crises — not because the underlying loss is unmanageable, but because no one else knows how the role actually functions.

Why succession planning is neglected

Succession planning is rarely urgent until the moment it becomes critical, which means it consistently loses out to more immediate daily demands. Most Kenyan schools operate with significant institutional knowledge concentrated in a small number of senior staff, with little documentation or deliberate development of potential successors.

Documenting how key roles actually work

A simple, practical exercise — asking each senior staff member (deputy principal, key HODs, the bursar) to document the core processes and responsibilities of their role in a brief written guide — creates a resource that dramatically eases any future transition, whether planned or sudden. This does not need to be elaborate; a clear list of recurring tasks, key contacts, and where relevant information is stored is often sufficient.

Practical starting point: Ask each senior staff member: "If you were unexpectedly unavailable for a month starting tomorrow, what would someone need to know to keep your responsibilities running?" Document the answer. This single exercise, repeated across senior roles, builds meaningful institutional resilience.

Identifying and developing potential successors

Rather than only looking externally when a senior vacancy arises, principals who identify promising staff early and deliberately expose them to relevant responsibilities — delegating specific deputy-level tasks to a strong senior teacher, involving a department member in HOD-level decisions — build genuine internal capacity that reduces dependency on any single individual.

Cross-training for critical functions

Certain functions — fee management, examination coordination, timetable administration — are particularly disruptive if concentrated in one person with no backup understanding of the system. Ensuring at least one other staff member has working familiarity with these critical functions, even without full responsibility for them, provides essential continuity if the primary person is suddenly unavailable.

Managing planned transitions well

Where a senior staff departure is known in advance — an approaching retirement, a confirmed transfer — a structured handover period, where the outgoing and incoming staff member work alongside each other for at least a few weeks, transfers practical knowledge far more effectively than a handover reduced to written notes alone.

The digital systems advantage

Much of the institutional knowledge that used to exist only in a senior staff member's head — student histories, fee records, assessment data, timetable logic — is far more resilient to staff transitions when it lives in a well-maintained digital system accessible to appropriate staff, rather than in personal files, memory, or informal notes that leave with the departing individual.

Keep institutional knowledge in the system, not just in people's heads.
